For commercial re-use, please contact journals.permissions@oup.com.</license-p></license></permissions><self-uri xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" content-type="pmc-pdf" xlink:href="ofw011.pdf"/><self-uri xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" content-type="pdf" xlink:href="ofw011.pdf"/><abstract abstract-type="precis"><p>Antibiotic-associated diarrhea is an important clinical problem, associated with morbidity, mortality and healthcare costs. Our randomized, placebo controlled multicenter trial do not support the efficacy of <italic toggle="yes">Saccharomyces boulardii</italic> in the prevention of antibiotic-associated diarrhea.</p></abstract><abstract><p><bold><italic toggle="yes">Background.</italic></bold> Antibiotic-associated diarrhea (AAD) and <italic toggle="yes">Clostridium difficile</italic>-associated diarrhea (CDAD) are common complications of antibiotic use. Data on the efficacy of probiotics to prevent AAD and CDAD are unclear. We aimed to evaluate the efficacy of <italic toggle="yes">Saccharomyces boulardii</italic> to prevent AAD and CDAD in hospitalized adult patients.</p><p><bold><italic toggle="yes">Methods.</italic></bold> We conducted a multicenter, phase III, double-masked, randomized, placebo-controlled trial in hospitalized patients who received systemic antibiotic treatment in 15 hospitals in Germany between July 2010 and October 2012. Participants received Perenterol forte 250 mg capsules or matching placebo twice per day within 24 hours of initiating antibiotic treatment, continued treatment for 7 days after antibiotic discontinuation, and were then observed for 6 weeks.</p><p><bold><italic toggle="yes">Results.</italic></bold> Two thousand four hundred forty-four patients were screened. The trial was stopped early for futility after inclusion of 477 participants. Two hundred forty-six patients aged 60.1 ± 16.5 years and 231 patients aged 56.5 ± 17.8 were randomized to the <italic toggle="yes">S boulardii</italic> group and the placebo group, respectively, with 21 and 19 AADs in the respective groups (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = .87). The hazard ratio of AAD in the <italic toggle="yes">S boulardii</italic> group compared with the placebo group was 1.02 (95% confidence interval, .55–1.90; <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = .94). <italic toggle="yes">Clostridium difficile</italic>-associated diarrhea occurred in 0.8% of participants (4 of 477). Nine serious adverse events were recorded in the <italic toggle="yes">S boulardii</italic> group, and 3 serious adverse events were recorded in the placebo group. None were related to study participation.</p><p><bold><italic toggle="yes">Conclusions.</italic></bold> We found no evidence for an effect of <italic toggle="yes">S boulardii</italic> in preventing AAD or CDAD in a population of hospitalized patients without particular risk factors apart from systemic antibiotic treatment.</p><p><bold><italic toggle="yes">ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier.</italic></bold> <ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="pmc:clinical-trial" xlink:href="NCT01143272">NCT01143272</ext-link>.</p></abstract><kwd-group><kwd>antibiotic-associated diarrhea</kwd><kwd><italic toggle="yes">Clostridium difficile</italic>-associated diarrhea</kwd><kwd>probiotic</kwd><kwd>randomized controlled trial</kwd><kwd><italic toggle="yes">Saccharomyces boulardii</italic></kwd></kwd-group><funding-group><award-group Institute for Tropical Medicine and the University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf</funding-source></award-group></funding-group><counts><page-count BY-NC-ND</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>cover-date</meta-name><meta-value>Winter 2016</meta-value></custom-meta></custom-meta-group></article-meta></front><body><p>Antibiotic-associated diarrhea (AAD) refers to otherwise unexplained diarrhea that occurs in association with the administration of antibiotics. It has been reported to occur in up to one third of patients receiving antibiotics [<xref rid="OFW011C1" ref-type="bibr">1</xref>–<xref rid="OFW011C3" ref-type="bibr">3</xref>]. The most severe form is <italic toggle="yes">Clostridium difficile</italic>-associated diarrhea (CDAD). Consequences of AAD and CDAD include increased morbidity [<xref rid="OFW011C4" ref-type="bibr">4</xref>, <xref rid="OFW011C5" ref-type="bibr">5</xref>] and mortality, extended hospital stays, an increased risk of developing complications such as colitis or toxic megacolon, discontinuation of the needed antibiotic, and higher healthcare cost.</p><p>Bacterial preparations and yeast are used widely for different indications. Sales grow globally by approximately 7% per year and are predicted to be $48 billion by 2017 [<xref rid="OFW011C6" ref-type="bibr">6</xref>]. Prevention of AAD is a common indication. Based on the hypothesized dysbiosis of the gut microbiome due to antibiotics [<xref rid="OFW011C1" ref-type="bibr">1</xref>], coadministering yeast or bacterial preparations for preventive purposes may help re-establishing the disrupted intestinal microflora, enhancing immune responses, lowering colonic pH favoring the growth of nonpathogenic bacteria, and clearing pathogens and their toxins from the host [<xref rid="OFW011C7" ref-type="bibr">7</xref>, <xref rid="OFW011C8" ref-type="bibr">8</xref>]. The nonpathogenic, live yeast <italic toggle="yes">Saccharomyces cerevisiae</italic> var <italic toggle="yes">boulardii</italic> (<italic toggle="yes">S boulardii</italic>) has been favorably discussed because it has an excellent safety profile and is not subject to the effects of concurrently administered antibiotics. However, some cases of generalized fungal infections occurring under unfavorable circumstances have been described [<xref rid="OFW011C9" ref-type="bibr">9</xref>].</p><p>Despite some evidence suggesting that <italic toggle="yes">S boulardii</italic> may reduce the relative risk of AAD by approximately 60% [<xref rid="OFW011C10" ref-type="bibr">10</xref>, <xref rid="OFW011C11" ref-type="bibr">11</xref>], the quality of the data is still weak. Heterogeneity, high risk of bias, and small sample sizes limit the interpretation of findings. Because of the increasing clinical importance of AAD and CDAD [<xref rid="OFW011C12" ref-type="bibr">12</xref>, <xref rid="OFW011C13" ref-type="bibr">13</xref>] and encouraging yet inconclusive data, we tested the efficacy of Perenterol forte 250 mg capsules in addition to any antibiotic treatment for reducing the hazard of AAD in hospitalized patients in Germany. To address a broad patient group, we did not restrict the sample to a specific at-risk group such as the elderly. Because the effects of yeast and microbial preparations may be strain-specific [<xref rid="OFW011C14" ref-type="bibr">14</xref>], we did not administer a mix of strains.</p><sec sec-type="methods" id="s2"><title>METHODS</title><sec id="s2a"><title>Study Overview and Ethics</title><p>Between June 2010 and October 2012, we conducted a multicenter, double-masked, randomized, placebo-controlled trial in hospitalized patients who received systemic antibiotic treatment. Seventeen academic hospitals across Germany participated in the trial, and 15 hospitals recruited 477 patients, whereas 2 hospitals recruited none. The trial was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Chamber of Physicians of Hamburg (reference: PVN 3440 on April 19, 2010) and the ethics committees of the participating clinical centers. The trial was conducted according to the Declaration of Helsinki.
</p></sec><sec id="s2b"><title>Study Population</title><p>Inclusion and exclusion criteria are reported in Table <xref ref-type="table" rid="OFW011TB1">1</xref>. Any eligible patient was informed in writing about the trial procedures, goals, and potential risks. If the patient was willing to participate in the trial, he/she signed the informed consent form.
<table-wrap id="OFW011TB1" orientation="portrait" position="float"><label>Table 1.</label><caption><p>Inclusion and exclusion criteria for the SacBo trial</p></caption><table frame="hsides" rules="groups"><colgroup span="1"><col align="left" span="1"/></colgroup><tbody><tr><td rowspan="1" colspan="1">Inclusion criteria:</td></tr><tr><td rowspan="1" colspan="1">
<list list-type="bullet"><list-item><p>adult patient (≥18 years old) hospitalized in the trial center</p></list-item><list-item><p>systemic antibiotic treatment</p></list-item><list-item><p>legally competent</p></list-item><list-item><p>able to follow the trial procedures</p></list-item><list-item><p>signed informed consent</p></list-item></list></td></tr><tr><td rowspan="1" colspan="1">Exclusion criteria:</td></tr><tr><td rowspan="1" colspan="1">
<list list-type="bullet"><list-item><p>hypersensitivity to yeast and/or Perenterol<sup>®</sup> forte and/or placebo and/or its ingredients: <italic toggle="yes">Saccharomyces cerevisiae</italic> HANSEN CBS 5926 (<italic toggle="yes">boulardii</italic>), lactose-monohydrate, magnesium stearate, gelatin, sodium dodecyl sulfate, titanium dioxide, microcrystalline cellulose</p></list-item><list-item><p>central venous catheter (currently or likely during the course of the trial)</p></list-item><list-item><p>immunosuppression, particularly: known malignant tumor or current cytostatic chemotherapy or chemotherapy planned during the antibiotic intake or cytostatic chemotherapy within the last 4 weeks; radiation therapy in the past 4 weeks, current or planned during the course of the antibiotic treatment; systemic immunosuppressive treatment (i.e. after organ transplant or with rheumatic disorder) – topical or inhaled steroids were permitted; known HIV infection</p></list-item><list-item><p>current and/or chronic diarrhea</p></list-item><list-item><p>regular intake of products containing <italic toggle="yes">Sac. boulardii</italic> in the 7 days before inclusion into the trial</p></list-item><list-item><p>systemic antimycotic treatment</p></list-item><list-item><p>systemic antibiotic treatment in the past 6 weeks</p></list-item><list-item><p>no birth control for the duration of the trial for women of reproductive age (failure proportion &lt;1%/year), pregnancy, or breastfeeding</p></list-item><list-item><p>simultaneous participation in other clinical trials</p></list-item></list></td></tr></tbody></table></table-wrap></p></sec><sec id="s2c"><title>Randomization, Concealment, and Masking</title><p>A blocked randomization stratified by center with an allocation ratio of 1:1 was performed using a computer-assisted method. The allocation sequence was generated by an independent statistician and concealed from any participant or member of the study team until the databases were locked. Allocation concealment was achieved by an internet-based central treatment allocation. For emergency purposes, a sealed, opaque envelope in each center contained allocation information for each participant in that center. Participants, study staff, and data analysts were masked to treatment assignment.</p></sec><sec id="s2d"><title>Antibiotic Treatment</title><p>The basic treatment in both trial arms was systemic antibiotics according to the predetermined treatment approach. The antibiotics were from the groups outlined in panel <ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="uri" xlink:href="http://ofid.oxfordjournals.org/lookup/suppl/doi:10.1093/ofid/ofw011/-/DC1">(See Supplementary Data)</ext-link>. The treatment could include more than 1 antibiotic.</p></sec><sec id="s2e"><title>Trial Intervention</title><p>The trial medication was Perenterol forte 250 mg capsules (containing at least 1.8 × 10<sup>10</sup> live cells/g lyophilisate) or a matching placebo administrated orally twice per day. In treatment phase I (Figure <xref ref-type="fig" rid="OFW011F1">1</xref>), which was of variable duration, the trial medication was given simultaneously with any systemic antibiotic. The trial medication was started immediately after the first-time administration of an antibiotic. The mean time until start of the study medication was half a day (range, 0–2 days; standard deviation = .5 days). When the antibiotic treatment was discontinued, the participant started treatment phase II and took the trial medication for 7 more days. However, the maximum treatment duration was 8 weeks. When, during treatment phase II, a new antibiotic was prescribed, the participant returned to treatment phase I. This happened in 44 participants, 23 (9.4%) in the <italic toggle="yes">S boulardii</italic> group and 21 (9.1%) in the placebo group. After treatment phase II, the participant was observed for 6 weeks. Drug accountability was done by counting capsules that were returned to the data coordinating center. The consistency of each bowel movement as well as the stool frequency was recorded by the participant herself/himself in the participant's diary. Outcome data were collected by weekly telephone interviews and review of the diary, the prespecified source document.
<fig id="OFW011F1" orientation="portrait" position="float"><label>Figure 1.</label><caption><p>Study flow. Abbreviation: <italic toggle="yes">Sac</italic>., <italic toggle="yes">Saccharomyces</italic>.</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="ofw01101.jpg"/></fig></p></sec><sec id="s2f"><title>Study Outcomes</title><p>Previous trials suffered from inconsistent definitions for diarrhea. Therefore, we prespecified 3 definitions. The World Health Organization (WHO) defines diarrhea as the passage of 3 or more loose or liquid stools (mostly in larger amounts) within 24 hours (<uri xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="http://www.who.int/topics/diarrhoea/en/">http://www.who.int/topics/diarrhoea/en/</uri>). Our main definition was more stringent. Participants had to fulfill the above definition for at least 2 days (“modified WHO definition”). Our third definition was the WHO definition lasting at least 5 days (“severe diarrhea definition”). Only 1 participant fulfilled this definition. Antibiotic-associated diarrhea was defined as diarrhea with onset not before the third day of antibiotic treatment. <italic toggle="yes">Clostridium difficile</italic>-associated diarrhea was defined as AAD plus detection of <italic toggle="yes">C difficile</italic> toxin A and/or B in the stool, or of toxin producing <italic toggle="yes">C difficile</italic> in the stool using polymerase chain reaction, or of typical membranes in colonoscopy or sigmoidoscopy.</p><p>The primary outcome was the risk of AAD expressed as hazard ratios. Secondary outcomes were as follows: risk of CDAD; risk of AAD without signs of CDAD; risk of CDAD among all AAD patients; association of AAD with increased initial leukocyte count and C-reactive protein (CRP); association of CDAD with increased initial leukocyte count and CRP; incidence density of AAD or CDAD; average duration of AAD or CDAD; average stool frequency in patients with AAD or CDAD; hazard of a discontinuation or change of the initially administered antibiotic, respectively.</p></sec><sec id="s2g"><title>Statistical Analysis</title><p>A 15% incidence of AAD was assumed for the placebo group while on antibiotic treatment. 686 patients would be needed in each group for 80% power to detect 5% difference in the cumulative incidence of AAD between treatment groups. We planned to include 1520 patients to account for losses to follow-up.</p><p>Due to slow recruitment and unexpectedly few events, an unplanned, masked interim analysis according to the Müller and Schäfer [<xref rid="OFW011C15" ref-type="bibr">15</xref>] procedure was carried out as suggested by the principal investigator (S. E.) jointly with the Data Safety and Monitoring Board. The conditional power was estimated based on a simulation of the conditional rejection error probability, assuming consistent recruitment of 300 additional participants and treatment effect. We prespecified that the study would only continue if the conditional power was at least 70%. When the conditional power was estimated to be approximately 10.5% in October 2012, the trial was stopped for futility after recruitment had been paused since September 2012. This analysis is based on data of 477 participants who were recruited and observed until trial termination.</p><p>Data were analyzed for each of the 3 diarrhea definitions and according to the intention-to-treat principle (ITT). The ITT population included all participants as randomized. Per-protocol (PP) analyses were performed as part of extensive sensitivity analyses (<ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="uri" xlink:href="http://ofid.oxfordjournals.org/lookup/suppl/doi:10.1093/ofid/ofw011/-/DC1">Supplementary Appendix</ext-link>). The PP population excluded participants with missing data and those who deviated from the protocol or were erroneously included. Safety parameters were evaluated “as-treated”, including all participants who have received at least 1 dose of trial medication.</p><p>Survival analysis was done to estimate the efficacy of <italic toggle="yes">S boulardii</italic> to reduce the hazard of AAD (primary endpoint) using all available data. A recurrent event Cox proportional hazards model (Prentice, Williams, and Peterson model) [<xref rid="OFW011C16" ref-type="bibr">16</xref>] was constructed to evaluate the overall hazard ratio (HR) of AAD comparing both groups. Participants were censored if they did not have AAD by the end of the observation period or were lost to follow-up. Log rank test was used to compare the number of AADs in the <italic toggle="yes">S boulardii</italic> and the placebo group. Finally, we calculated a covariate adjusted Cox regression model adjusting for center, age, sex, duration of antibiotic treatment, and readministration of antibiotics after completion of treatment phase I. All analyses using the WHO definition are presented in the <ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="uri" xlink:href="http://ofid.oxfordjournals.org/lookup/suppl/doi:10.1093/ofid/ofw011/-/DC1">Supplementary Appendix</ext-link>.</p><p>For secondary endpoints, a Cox proportional hazard model was used to evaluate the HR of CDAD; participants having AAD without signs of CDAD; participants having CDAD among all AAD patients; and discontinuation or change of the initial antibiotic comparing the 2 groups. The associations between AAD and leukocyte count and CRP were assessed in the Cox regression model.</p><p>The protocol prespecified that the primary and secondary endpoints be analyzed using a Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel χ<sup>2</sup> test. Because approximately half of the study participants had some missing observations, the prespecified statistical approach would have resulted in an inefficient analysis of only participants with complete data. We present these results in the <ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="uri" xlink:href="http://ofid.oxfordjournals.org/lookup/suppl/doi:10.1093/ofid/ofw011/-/DC1">Supplementary Appendix</ext-link>. In short, the results of both analytic techniques are similar. Inverse probability weighting did not suggest selection bias by differential losses to follow-up. The trial is registered: ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: <ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="pmc:clinical-trial" xlink:href="NCT01143272">NCT01143272</ext-link>.</p></sec></sec><sec sec-type="results" id="s3"><title>RESULTS</title><p>Two thousand four hundred forty-four patients were screened, and 1967 were ineligible or unwilling to participate (Figure <xref ref-type="fig" rid="OFW011F2">2</xref>). Two hundred forty-six and 231 patients were randomized to the active treatment and placebo groups, respectively. Three study participants (1 in the placebo and 2 in the <italic toggle="yes">S boulardii</italic> group) erroneously received the wrong medication. This was corrected within 2 days. One hundred eighty-five participants (100 in the <italic toggle="yes">S boulardii</italic> group and 85 in the placebo group) did not document their daily stools completely throughout the observation period. The data of all 477 patients were used for the ITT analysis, whereas 292 patients (61%) with complete observations were included in the PP analysis.
<fig id="OFW011F2" orientation="portrait" position="float"><label>Figure 2.</label><caption><p>Enrollment, randomization, and follow-up. Abbreviations: <italic toggle="yes">Sac</italic>., <italic toggle="yes">Saccharomyces</italic>.</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="ofw01102.jpg"/></fig></p><p>The baseline characteristics of study participants were comparable between groups in the ITT and PP populations (Table <xref ref-type="table" rid="OFW011TB2">2</xref> and <ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="uri" xlink:href="http://ofid.oxfordjournals.org/lookup/suppl/doi:10.1093/ofid/ofw011/-/DC1">Supplementary Appendix Table 1</ext-link>). Table <xref ref-type="table" rid="OFW011TB3">3</xref> shows antibiotic treatment by class and treatment assignment.

(64.5%)</td></tr><tr><td rowspan="1" colspan="1"> 2 classes</td><td rowspan="1" colspan="1">93 (37.8%)</td><td rowspan="1" colspan="1">82 (35.5%)</td></tr></tbody></table></table-wrap></p><sec id="s3a"><title>Primary Endpoint</title><p>Forty cases of AAD occurred in 425 study participants, and the total time at risk was 19 165 days. Twenty-one and 19 AADs happened in the <italic toggle="yes">S boulardii</italic> group and the placebo group, respectively (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = .87). The mean number of episodes of AADs is shown in Table <xref ref-type="table" rid="OFW011TB4">4</xref>. The HR of AAD in the <italic toggle="yes">S boulardii</italic> group compared with the placebo group was 1.02 (95% CI, .55–1.90; <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = .94). None of the prespecified factors (center, age, sex, duration of antibiotic treatment, and readministration of antibiotics after completion of treatment phase I) were associated with risk of AAD.
<table-wrap id="OFW011TB4" orientation="portrait" position="float"><label>Table 4.</label><caption><p>Number of Study Participants With 0, 1, or 2 Episodes of Antibiotic-Associated Diarrhea</p></caption><table frame="hsides" rules="groups"><colgroup span="1"><col align="left" span="1"/><col align="char" char=" " span="1"/><col align="char" char="(" span="1"/><col align="char" char="." span="1"/><col align="char" char="(" span="1"/><col align="char" char="(" span="1"/><col align="char" char="." span="1"/></colgroup><thead><tr><th align="left" rowspan="2" colspan="1">Number 146)</th><th align="left" rowspan="1" colspan="1"><italic toggle="yes">P</italic> Value</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td rowspan="1" colspan="1">0</td><td rowspan="1" colspan="1">225 (91.5%)</td><td rowspan="1" colspan="1">214 (92.6%)</td><td rowspan="1" colspan="1">.25</td><td rowspan="1" colspan="1">130 (91.1%)</td><td rowspan="1" colspan="1">133 (89.0%)</td><td rowspan="1" colspan="1">16 (11.0%)</td><td rowspan="1" colspan="1">11 (7.5%)</td><td rowspan="1" colspan="1"/></tr><tr><td rowspan="1" colspan="1">2</td><td rowspan="1" colspan="1">0</td><td rowspan="1" colspan="1">2 (0.9%)</td><td rowspan="1" colspan="1"/><td rowspan="1" colspan="1">0</td><td rowspan="1" colspan="1">2 (1.4%)</td><td rowspan="1" colspan="1"/></tr></tbody></table><table-wrap-foot><fn id="tblfn2"><p>Abbreviations: AAD, antibiotic-associated diarrhea; ITT, intention-to-treat; PP, per-protocol.</p></fn></table-wrap-foot></table-wrap></p></sec><sec id="s3b"><title>Secondary Endpoints</title><p>Overall, 4 cases (0.8%) of CDAD were observed: two occurred in the <italic toggle="yes">S boulardii</italic> group and 2 in the placebo group. Due to the small number of CDAD cases, the planned analyses were not performed. Thirty-six cases of AAD without signs of CDAD occurred in 421 participants, and the total time at risk was 18 483 days. The HR of AAD without signs of CDAD in the <italic toggle="yes">S boulardii</italic> group compared with the placebo group was 0.92 (95% CI, .49–1.73; <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = .80). In a multivariate Cox model adjusting for age, sex, CRP, leukocyte count, duration of antibiotic treatment, and administration of antibiotics, the HR of AAD without signs of CDAD in the <italic toggle="yes">S boulardii</italic> group compared with the placebo group was 1.03 (95% CI, .53–2.03; <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = .93). Of AAD cases per year, 0.78 and 0.64 were observed in the <italic toggle="yes">S boulardii</italic> group and the placebo group, respectively (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = .33). The mean duration of an AAD was 4.48 days in the <italic toggle="yes">S boulardii</italic> group and 4.26 days in the placebo group (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = .79). The mean frequency of loose or liquid stools per day of AAD was slightly higher in the <italic toggle="yes">S boulardii</italic> group compared with the placebo group (4.48 vs 4.07, respectively; <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = .18). The mean time to onset of AAD was 18.4 days in the <italic toggle="yes">S boulardii</italic> group and 18.9 days in the placebo group (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = .87). Fourteen participants in the <italic toggle="yes">S boulardii</italic> group and 7 in the placebo group changed initial antibiotics (6.4% vs 3.4%, <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = .15). Antibiotic treatment had to be stopped in 2 participants in the <italic toggle="yes">S boulardii</italic> group and in 1 participant in the placebo group due to an AAD or CDAD (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = .67). Given these small numbers, we did not conduct further analyses.
</p></sec><sec id="s3c"><title>Adverse Events</title><p>Ten participants did not take any study drug and were therefore excluded from the safety analysis. Eighteen of 245 (7.3%) participants in the <italic toggle="yes">S boulardii</italic> group and 12 of 222 (5.4%) participants in placebo group had at least 1 adverse event (AE) (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> = .39). Overall, we recorded 36 AEs (24 in the <italic toggle="yes">S boulardii</italic> and 12 in the placebo group). Three and 5 AEs in the <italic toggle="yes">S boulardii</italic> and placebo group, respectively, were suspected to be causally related to the trial drug. The 3 AEs in the <italic toggle="yes">S boulardii</italic> group were as follows: 1 abdominal cramps, 1 flatulence, and 1 nausea, vomiting, and decreased appetite. The 5 AEs in the placebo group were as follows: 1 abdominal pain, 2 cases of nausea, 1 increased temperature, and 1 allergic exanthema. Nine serious AEs (SAEs) happened in the <italic toggle="yes">S boulardii</italic> group: 3 gastrointestinal disorders, 1 cardiac death, 1 cholecystitis, 2 cases of bacterial sepsis, 1 pulmonary empyema, and 1 renal failure. Three SAEs happened in the placebo group: 1 decompensated liver cirrhosis, 1 bronchial carcinoma, and 1 renal failure. None of the SAEs were related to the study drug.</p></sec></sec><sec sec-type="discussion" id="s4"><title>DISCUSSION</title><p>Hospitalized patients exposed to antibiotics are at risk of AAD. However, estimates about the incidence vary widely [<xref rid="OFW011C10" ref-type="bibr">10</xref>]. Antibiotic-associated diarrhea, although mostly mild and transient, is responsible for increased morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs. Several strategies have been put forward to prevent AAD and CDAD in healthcare settings, among which the coadministration of yeast or microbial preparations (“probiotics”) is thought to be promising.</p><p>We found no statistical difference between the risk of AAD in the <italic toggle="yes">S boulardii</italic> and the placebo group. The <italic toggle="yes">S boulardii</italic> group had a slightly higher but not statistically significant incidence density of AAD, longer duration of AAD, and higher frequency of loose stools during a diarrhea episode than the placebo group. The findings were robust in the PP as well as several sensitivity analyses (<ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="uri" xlink:href="http://ofid.oxfordjournals.org/lookup/suppl/doi:10.1093/ofid/ofw011/-/DC1">Supplementary Appendix</ext-link>). Age, sex, administration of additional antibiotics, duration of the antibiotic treatment, leukocyte count, and CRP levels were not associated with AAD risk. In this study, CDAD was rare.</p><p>The incidence of AAD and CDAD in our study was lower than suggested previously [<xref rid="OFW011C17" ref-type="bibr">17</xref>–<xref rid="OFW011C19" ref-type="bibr">19</xref>] but in line with the recently published large PLACIDE trial [<xref rid="OFW011C20" ref-type="bibr">20</xref>]. We calculated the number of episodes based on patient-reported stool frequency and consistency instead of asking directly about diarrhea, a concept with substantial interperson variability. Another reason for this low incidence may be that our study population was relatively young. We did not target a specific at-risk population. We may also have missed AAD and CDAD cases due to attrition, despite all our efforts to stay in touch with participants.</p><p>Some previous studies and systematic reviews indicated the efficacy of yeast or microbial preparations to prevent AAD or CDAD, reduce the duration of diarrhea, or reduce stool frequency during a diarrhea episode [<xref rid="OFW011C3" ref-type="bibr">3</xref>, <xref rid="OFW011C11" ref-type="bibr">11</xref>, <xref rid="OFW011C21" ref-type="bibr">21</xref>, <xref rid="OFW011C22" ref-type="bibr">22</xref>]. However, studies varied greatly regarding study population (age, disease severity), type of probiotic, and duration of treatment, probiotic dose, the definition of the outcome, and follow-up duration. The large PLACIDE trial did not find a lower frequency of AAD or CDAD in elderly inpatients after the administration of <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacilli</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">Bifidobacteria</italic> [<xref rid="OFW011C20" ref-type="bibr">20</xref>]. However, caution is needed when extrapolating data from bacterial preparations to yeast or of one strain to another because effects may be strain-specific [<xref rid="OFW011C23" ref-type="bibr">23</xref>]. Two systematic reviews suggested a specific beneficial effect of <italic toggle="yes">S boulardii</italic> [<xref rid="OFW011C24" ref-type="bibr">24</xref>, <xref rid="OFW011C25" ref-type="bibr">25</xref>]. Yet, the trials included in the systematic reviews were of substantial heterogeneity, and some had a high risk of bias. Some randomized controlled trials (RCTs) failed to find a beneficial effect of the yeast. Pozzoni et al [<xref rid="OFW011C17" ref-type="bibr">17</xref>] conducted a trial in 275 older inpatients in Italy and found the administration of <italic toggle="yes">S boulardii</italic> ineffective for reducing AAD and CDAD. We believe that the mechanism of action of “probiotic substances” needs to be understood much better before conducting further expensive RCTs.</p><p>This trial was stopped early for futility. Among the 2444 patients that we screened, 1967 (80.5%) were ineligible or not willing to participate. The most common reasons for ineligibility were immunosuppression, inability to follow study procedures, current or chronic diarrhea, and systemic antibiotic treatment in the past 6 weeks. It is clear that recruiting in large University Hospitals with a high proportion of very sick patients was a prime reason for the recruitment difficulties. Moreover, the patients who were eligible may have been relatively healthy resulting in few events. These practical difficulties need to be considered when designing trials in future.</p><p>This is the largest RCT to investigate the efficacy of <italic toggle="yes">S boulardii</italic> for the prevention of AAD. Nevertheless, this study has limitations. First, 1967 of 2444 screened patients were ineligible for participation. This may limit the external validity of the trial. Yet, approximately one third of these noninclusions were due to contraindications listed by the manufacturer. Others were due to ethical or operational constraints. Only 15% of screened patients declined to participate. Second, a large proportion of participants did not completely document stool frequencies and were thus excluded from the prespecified analysis (<ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="uri" xlink:href="http://ofid.oxfordjournals.org/lookup/suppl/doi:10.1093/ofid/ofw011/-/DC1">Supplementary Appendix</ext-link>). However, the survival analysis reported here used all available data, and multiple sensitivity analyses as well as the prespecified analysis showed consistent, robust results (<ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="uri" xlink:href="http://ofid.oxfordjournals.org/lookup/suppl/doi:10.1093/ofid/ofw011/-/DC1">Supplementary Appendix</ext-link>). In short, we compared the characteristics of participants who had complete data and those who had not, and there were no significant differences between the 2 groups except for CRP levels. We did several sensitivity analyses imputing different, extreme scenarios. We imputed all patients with missing data as (1) having the primary outcome (AAD) and (2) not having the primary outcome. We also performed inverse probability weighting to assess the impact of missing data. All sensitivity analyses revealed consistent results and did not suggest an effect of <italic toggle="yes">S boulardii</italic> (<ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="uri" xlink:href="http://ofid.oxfordjournals.org/lookup/suppl/doi:10.1093/ofid/ofw011/-/DC1">Supplementary Appendix</ext-link>)<italic toggle="yes">.</italic> We performed all analyses using the modified WHO definition as well as the WHO definition of diarrhea as outcome, and we did not find a difference between both groups. Third, we did not record previous hospital admission and previous gastrointestinal surgery, which may be risk factors for AAD [<xref rid="OFW011C2" ref-type="bibr">2</xref>]. However, randomization should distribute measured and unmeasured confounders evenly between the 2 groups. In addition, this is one of the few studies that rigorously administered <italic toggle="yes">S boulardii</italic> while taking antibiotics and 1 week thereafter and then observed participants over 6 weeks. This tedious regimen may have contributed to the relatively high proportion of participants with some missing data. Finally, we may have missed treatment effects due to a type-2 error. We reached only one third of the projected sample size with respective consequences for the power of the trial. However, based on our observed incidence of AAD in the 2 groups, if we had reached the targeted sample size, we still would not have found a difference between the groups.</p></sec><sec sec-type="conclusions" id="s5"><title>CONCLUSIONS</title><p>In conclusion, we found no evidence for the efficacy of the tested <italic toggle="yes">S boulardii</italic> regimen to prevent AAD in a population of hospitalized patients who received systemic antibiotic treatment.</p></sec><sec sec-type="supplementary-material" id="s6"><title>Supplementary Data</title><p><ext-link <article-title><italic toggle="yes">Saccharomyces boulardii</italic> for the prevention of antibiotic-associated diarrhea in adult hospitalized patients: a single-center, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial</article-title>. <source>Am J Gastroenterol</source>
